en: Theragāthā 6.12 Chakkanipāta,
Paṭhamavagga (First Chapter)
The Verses of the Elder Brahmadatta:
“Whence can there be anger for one who is without anger,
who is self-controlled and lives in equanimity?”
For one who is liberated through right knowledge,
who is tranquil and steadfast—
that very person is worse for that [offense].
He who does not retaliate against one who is angry conquers a battle that is difficult to win— the one who, when another is angry, remains without anger.
He acts for the benefit of both,
himself and the other; having recognized that the other is provoked to anger, [he remains calm].
He who, being mindful, brings peace to both—
treating both himself and another.
Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma think,
"He is a fool," even if anger should arise within them.
Reflect on the simile of the saw;
if craving for flavors should arise,
remember the simile of the son’s flesh.
If your mind runs toward sensual pleasures and states of existence,
restrain it quickly with mindfulness.
“… like a crab, difficult to catch.
… The Elder Brahmadatta …
